# **1\. Overview / Background** {#1.-overview-/-background}

London households push electricity demand to its daily peak on weekday evenings, when people come home to cook and run appliances. UK Power Networks, the operator of London's distribution network, has to size cables and substations for that peak, even though demand stays below it for most of the day. Under time-of-use (ToU) pricing, a supplier charges more when the network is under strain and less when it has spare capacity, so households have a reason to move their consumption.

UK Power Networks tested this idea in the Low Carbon London project, with Imperial College London in charge of trial design and analysis and EDF Energy as the supplier running the tariff. Of the 5,566 households in the dataset, 1,123 received an experimental dynamic time-of-use (dToU) tariff throughout 2013, in the UK's first dynamic pricing trial for homes (Schofield et al., 2015). The dataset labels these households ToU. EDF Energy sent them a day-ahead price signal through an in-home display or text message, at one of three levels (UK Power Networks, n.d.): High (67.20p/kWh), Normal (11.76p/kWh) or Low (3.99p/kWh). The other 4,443 households stayed on a flat standard tariff (Std).

Our project uses the Kaggle dataset "Smart Meters in London" (jeanmidev, n.d.), a repackaged copy of the London Datastore release (UK Power Networks, n.d.). The smart meters logged consumption every half hour from November 2011 to February 2014, 167,817,021 readings in total. The project team recruited these households as a balanced sample of the Greater London population. A household file labels each home as Std or ToU and assigns it an ACORN socio-demographic group, and separate files add hourly weather and UK bank holidays.

### 

# **2\. Problem Statement** {#2.-problem-statement}

During a High price event, a dToU household paid 67.20p for each kWh, 5.7 times the Normal rate of 11.76p. Economists expect households to cut or shift consumption in those half-hours. A household can run the washing machine after 22:00 to save money, but it still cooks dinner at 19:00. Suppliers and network operators need a measured response before they rely on dynamic pricing in place of new cables and substations. Whether 1% or 10% of evening load shifts changes how much network capacity operators need to build. 

The dataset contains its own comparison group. Std households lived in the same city, faced the same weather on the same dates, and paid a flat price throughout. Because households opted in to dToU, the Std group is not a randomised control (Schofield et al., 2015); household fixed effects remove any fixed difference between the two groups. For each half-hour of the day, we compare the gap between dToU and Std consumption on High and Low event days with the same gap on Normal days. We treat the change in that gap, a difference-in-differences (DiD) estimate, as the price effect, because weather and holidays affect both groups in the same way. We repeat the comparison within each ACORN group (Affluent, Comfortable and Adversity) to test whether some groups respond more than others. A second DiD compares 2013 with the 2012 baseline to check whether the fixed evening peak (16:00–19:00) moved over the whole trial year, using only households with enough 2012 readings. Both comparisons require us to join 167.8 million half-hourly readings with the tariff calendar and the household file, so we run the pipeline on Spark. 

Thai households face a similar choice. MEA and PEA offer a residential TOU rate with peak prices from 09:00 to 22:00 on weekdays (EPPO, n.d.). A Thai family weighing that rate can use London's results to judge which loads it could move out of peak hours. The savings will differ in Thailand, where air conditioning drives demand and the peak window lasts 13 hours.

#  **3\. Data Description** {#3.-data-description}

The project uses the Smart Meters in London dataset, publicly available on Kaggle and based on data from the Low Carbon London project. The dataset contains household electricity consumption records together with household, tariff, weather, socio-demographic, and calendar information.

The Kaggle dataset does not include the dynamic Time-of-Use (dToU) price signal schedule. Therefore, the dToU tariff schedule is obtained separately from the original London Datastore release and is used together with the Kaggle dataset for the analysis.

The data is primarily structured time-series and tabular data stored in CSV format.

## **3.1 Source and Specifications** {#3.1-source-and-specifications}

* Source: Smart Meters in London dataset on Kaggle, based on the Low Carbon London project.  
* Additional source: London Data store release for the dToU price signal schedule.  
* Type: Structured time-series and tabular data.  
* Format: Primarily CSV in the original Kaggle release.   
  * After preprocessing, cleaned data will be converted to Apache Parquet for more efficient large-scale processing and querying.  
* Volume: Kaggle dataset version 21 occupies approximately 9.56 GiB (10.27 GB) on disk and contains 343 files.  
* Frequency: Electricity consumption is recorded at 30-minute intervals.  
* Main scale: The half-hourly electricity dataset contains 167,817,021 records across 112 CSV files. 

## **3.2 Dataset Components** {#3.2-dataset-components}

The project combines several related data sources for analysis.

* Half-hourly electricity consumption (`halfhourly_dataset`): This is the primary dataset for analyzing household electricity use over time. Each record contains `LCLid`, `tstp`, and `energy(kWh/hh)`. The dataset contains 167,817,021 records across 112 CSV files.   
* Half-hourly block data (`hhblock_dataset`): This dataset contains 3,469,352 records across 112 CSV files and occupies 1,594 MiB (about 1.56 GiB). Each household-day is represented by `LCLid`, `day`, and 48 half-hourly consumption columns from `hh_0` to `hh_47`. This representation is directly useful for daily load-profile analysis and clustering.   
* Household information (`informations_households.csv`): Contains `LCLid`, tariff type (`stdorToU`), ACORN classification, grouped ACORN category, and file-mapping information. This file allows household consumption data to be linked with tariff and socio-demographic information.   
* dToU price signal schedule: Contains the timing and price levels of the dynamic Time-of-Use tariff events. This schedule is not included in the Kaggle download and is obtained separately from the original London Datastore release.  
* Daily electricity consumption: Provides daily aggregated electricity statistics including mean, median, minimum, maximum, standard deviation, and total energy consumption.  
* Weather data: Includes hourly and daily weather information such as temperature, humidity, wind speed, and other weather conditions that can be aligned with electricity consumption.  
* ACORN details: Provides socio-demographic classification information associated with household groups.  
* UK bank holidays: Provides calendar information that can be used to identify holiday-related consumption patterns.

The Kaggle package contains separate folders for daily, half-hourly, and half-hour-block electricity data, together with household, ACORN, weather, and bank holiday files. 

## **3.3 Data Considerations** {#3.3-data-considerations}

The dataset is distributed across multiple related files rather than stored in a single table. Household information can be linked to electricity consumption using `LCLid`, while weather, bank holiday, and dToU price information can be aligned using timestamps or dates.

The dataset also contains 51 households without an ACORN group. These households should be excluded from analyses that compare electricity consumption behavior across ACORN socio-demographic groups. 

Detailed analysis of record counts, data types, missing values, and distributions is addressed separately in the General Statistics section.

The UK Data Service release of the same trial removed households with inside knowledge of the trial, a non-standard tariff such as Economy 7 before 2013, a replaced faulty meter or a withdrawal request, leaving 1,025 dToU and 4,173 non-dToU households (Schofield et al., 2015). The Kaggle release has no flag for these cases, so our 5,566 households may include some of them.

In the columns we use, the largest explicit gap is 5,560 "Null" readings, 0.003% of the half-hourly rows. Absent rows outnumber them. The daily layer lists 3,510,433 household-days, and at 48 readings each a full record would hold 168,500,784 half-hourly rows. The half-hourly layer holds 683,763 fewer (0.41%), more than 100 absent rows for every "Null" value, and all of them fall on the 41,081 incomplete household-days described in Section 4.4. Our cleaning step has to detect absent timestamps as well as null values.

## **4.4 Data Validity and Coverage** {#4.4-data-validity-and-coverage}

Most households joined between March and October 2012\. The number of Std households reporting rose from near zero in November 2011 to about 4,400 by October 2012, and ToU households followed the same path to about 1,100 (Figure 4.2). Both counts drifted down through 2013\. Because most households joined during 2012, the year-over-year comparison asks for at least 6 usable months of 2012, not a full year. Under the coverage rule in Section 5.1, 3,356 Std households (75.5%) and 835 ToU households (74.4%) have enough readings in both 2012 and 2013\. The event-level comparison needs 2013 alone, and 4,387 Std (98.7%) and 1,111 ToU households (98.9%) qualify for it. We use the event-level DiD as the primary estimate and keep the year-over-year DiD as a check on the 2012 subset. A complete household-day has 48 readings. Of the 3,510,433 household-days, 41,081 (1.17%) have fewer and 30 have none. Incomplete days peak when households join and when the data ends. In November 2011, 22.0% of household-days were incomplete, and the share rises again during the main joining period from April to June 2012 and in February 2014, the last month of data. Through 2013 it stays at about 1% or less (Figure 4.3). The hhblock layer is 41,081 rows shorter than the daily layer, matching the count of incomplete days, so we treat it as a table of complete household-days. ![][image3]

## **4.5 Sample Distributions** {#tariff-and-acorn-groups}

### **Tariff and ACORN groups** {#tariff-and-acorn-groups}

Of the 5,566 households, 4,443 (79.8%) stayed on the flat standard tariff and 1,123 (20.2%) received the dToU tariff (Figure 4.4). ACORN-E and ACORN-Q are the largest categories, with 1,567 households (28.2%) and 831 (14.9%). At group level the sample contains 2,192 Affluent, 1,507 Comfortable and 1,816 Adversity households (Figure 4.5).  
![][image5]![][image6]Tariff assignment differs across ACORN groups. Households opted in to dToU (Schofield et al., 2015), and 22.4% of Affluent and 21.4% of Comfortable households joined it, against 16.4% of Adversity households (χ² \= 23.95, df \= 2, p \= 6.3 × 10⁻⁶, excluding the 51 unclassified households; Figure 4.6). Household fixed effects absorb any fixed difference between ACORN groups, so Section 5 handles this imbalance by estimating the price effect separately within each ACORN group.![][image7]  
Figure 4.5: Households per ACORN category, coloured by ACORN group.

### **Time-of-day load profile** {#time-of-day-load-profile}

Across the 3,469,352 complete household-days in the hhblock layer, mean demand bottoms out at 0.113 kWh per half-hour at 04:00 and peaks at 0.321 kWh in the 19:00–19:30 slot, 2.8 times higher (Figure 4.7). Demand stays above 0.30 kWh for seven half-hours, from 18:00 to 21:30. The fixed 16:00–19:00 window in Section 5.1 contains two of those seven.

# **5\. Proposed Analytics Approach** {#5.-proposed-analytics-approach}

The London Smart Meters dataset holds half-hourly kWh readings from 5,566 households (Nov 2011–Feb 2014), with tariff type (Standard vs. ToU), ACORN classification, weather, and bank holidays.

We compare ToU households with Std households within the 2013 trial year, using the dynamic price events (High, Normal, Low) as the treatment. Because households were recruited progressively during 2012, not every ToU household has a full pre-trial year, so the main comparison is built on 2013 data alone; the 2012 baseline is used only for the households that have it. Pandas can summarise the 167,817,021 half-hourly readings one block file at a time (Section 4), but the analysis joins every reading with the half-hourly price schedule, weather and household file and rebuilds household-level features many times. We run these steps on Apache Spark, which reads the 112 block files in parallel, and we store the cleaned data as partitioned Parquet; Section 5.3 reports the query-time benchmark against raw CSV.

**Assumptions:** price events were announced a day ahead to ToU households only, so Std households in the same half-hours capture weather, holiday and time-of-day effects. Of the 1,123 ToU households, 835 (74.4%) have at least 6 usable months of 2012 readings and meet the 2013 rule (Section 4.4); this count sets how much weight the year-over-year comparison can carry.

## **5.1 Data Preprocessing**

1. **Data Ingestion & Storage:** Load half-hourly files into Spark as Parquet, partitioned by year and month; use Pandas for lighter, pre-aggregated files during EDA.

2. **Data Integration:** Join consumption with informations\_households.csv (tariff, ACORN), weather, and bank holidays via LCLid and timestamp; merge the dToU price schedule to label High/Normal/Low windows in 2013\.

3. **Cleaning & Missing Data:** Cast invalid values to NaN; treat a day as usable when it has at least 44 of 48 half-hourly readings, and a calendar day with no reading row as unusable; keep households with ≥90% usable days *within their own recorded period* in 2013 (a fixed 2012–2013 window would drop every household recruited after early 2012); flag households with ≥6 usable months in 2012 as the year-over-year subset, where a month is usable when at least 90% of its calendar days are usable; interpolate small gaps.

4. **Feature Engineering:**

   * Time: hour, half-hour index, weekday/weekend, month, season, holiday flag

   * Peak indicators: fixed evening peak (16:00–19:00) \+ dynamic High-price flag for 2013

   * Behavioral: total, peak-period, and peak-share consumption; Load Factor

   * Weather: Heating Degree Days as a seasonal control

5. **Normalization:** Scale daily load profiles by total usage so clustering captures consumption *shape*, not household size.

## **5.2 Analytical Techniques & Modeling**

1. **EDA:** Compare average load curves (ToU vs. Std) on High, Normal and Low event days in 2013, by season, weekend and ACORN group; check when each household came online and how much 2012 history it has; use heatmaps to spot patterns and outliers.

2. **Event-Level Comparison (main method):** For each half-hour, compare ToU consumption under High and Low prices with the same households under Normal prices, and subtract the same difference for Std households at the same moments: (ToU\_event − ToU\_normal) − (Std\_event − Std\_normal). Panel regression with household and half-hour fixed effects, controlling for temperature and holidays. This needs only 2013 data, so it uses every ToU household regardless of recruitment date.

3. **Rebound Analysis:** Measure consumption in the half-hours before and after each price event to see whether load is reduced or only shifted. Significance via Wilcoxon signed-rank test on household-level differences.

4. **Year-over-Year DiD (robustness check):** (ToU₂₀₁₃ − ToU₂₀₁₂) − (Std₂₀₁₃ − Std₂₀₁₂) on the subset with ≥6 usable months of 2012 data, with parallel trends tested on 2012\. The subset holds 835 ToU and 3,356 Std households (Section 4.4); it remains a check on the event-level estimate, not the primary estimate. STL decomposition and a SARIMA/Prophet counterfactual trained on the same subset cross-check the estimate.

5. **Clustering:** K-Means on normalized 2013 daily load profiles from Normal-price days (Elbow/Silhouette for k), grouping households into personas (e.g., evening peakers, flat consumers) and comparing cluster membership on Normal vs. High-price days; 2012-to-2013 transitions are tracked for the year-over-year subset.

   * **Classification:** Label households responsive/non-responsive by their event-level response; train Random Forest/XGBoost on features that do not depend on the price signal (ACORN, consumption on Normal-price days, Normal-day load-profile cluster, weather sensitivity estimated on Normal-price days), evaluated via F1/ROC-AUC, with SHAP for interpretability.

**5.3 Tools and platforms**

Sections 5.1 and 5.2 describe what the pipeline does; this section describes where each step runs and why each tool was chosen. All resources run on AWS in the us-east-1 region.

**Ingestion.** Amazon S3 serves as the raw landing zone. The 112 half-hourly block files, the supplementary files, and the dToU price schedule from the London Datastore are uploaded with the AWS CLI through AWS CloudShell. The existing block structure maps directly onto Spark partitions, allowing parallel reads without further splitting.

**Processing.** The preprocessing steps in Section 5.1 run as PySpark jobs on Amazon EMR, which provisions a managed Hadoop cluster with Spark executing on YARN and HDFS providing cluster-local storage during each job. S3 remains the persistent layer. We report the query time difference between the raw CSV and the partitioned Parquet layers as a measure of this stage.

**Why Spark and EMR.** Our exploratory statistics (Section 4\) streamed the half-hourly files through pandas one block at a time, which suffices for per-file counts but not for the pipeline itself: joining all 167.8 million readings to the household file and the half-hourly price schedule, computing coverage per household across files, and rewriting the layer as partitioned Parquet all require operations across blocks. Spark performs these as a single partitioned job. At this volume a small cluster offers limited speedup over one well-provisioned machine, so EMR's role is to show that the same job scales horizontally without code changes; the measured gain we report comes from the Parquet benchmark. 

**Analytics.** Spark reduces the half-hourly data to aggregated tables, and each method in Section 5.2 runs where its input size fits (Table 5.1).

*Table 5.1: Where each method runs*

| Method (Section 5.2)  | Input  | Tool  | Environment  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Usable-day rule, coverage flags  | Half-hourly, 167.8M rows  | PySpark  | EMR |
| K-Means, silhouette  | Normalised 2013 household-day profiles, up to \~1.9M rows; fit on Normal-price days only  | Spark MLlib  | EMR  |
| Event-level DiD  | Household × half-hour-of-day × price condition, \~800K rows  | linearmodels  | Single machine  |
| Year-over-year DiD  | Household-day, year-over-year subset  | linearmodels  | Single machine  |
| STL, SARIMA, Prophet  | Daily series, year-over-year subset  | statsmodels, Prophet  | Single machine  |
| Rebound significance  | Household-level differences, \~5.5K  | SciPy  | Single machine  |
| Responder classification  | Household features, \~5.5K  | scikit-learn, XGBoost, SHAP  | Single machine  |
| EDA and heatmaps  | Aggregated tables  | pandas, Matplotlib, seaborn  | Single machine  |

**Visualisation.** Amazon Athena queries the Parquet layer through the AWS Glue Data Catalog. A Streamlit dashboard presents load profiles, treatment effect estimates, and cluster segments. We chose Streamlit over Amazon QuickSight because QuickSight is not available in the AWS Academy Learner Lab.

**Development and cost management.** Code is version-controlled in GitHub and developed in PySpark local mode against a subset of block files before any cluster is provisioned. Full-dataset runs use EMR clusters of m4.large instances, created per job and terminated on completion, with all outputs written to S3 because clusters do not persist between lab sessions. The account budget is \$50, so cluster size and runtime are kept to the minimum each run needs.

# **6\. Expected Result or Insights** {#6.-expected-result-or-insights}

The analysis of the Low Carbon London smart meter dataset is designed to measure whether dynamic price signals change household electricity use, and to characterise the form and distribution of that change. All effects are measured against the flat-rate (Std) households as a control group. The following outputs and insights are expected:

## **6.1 Evening Peak Load Profile (Line Chart)** {#6.1-evening-peak-load-profile-(line-chart)}

* A line chart will show average half-hourly demand for the dToU and Std groups across the 24-hour cycle, in 2012 and 2013, for households with at least six usable months of 2012 readings. This is a secondary, year-over-year check. Its subset size is reported in Section 4.4, and the main price effect comes from the event comparison in Section 6.2.  
* This shows whether dToU households move consumption out of the fixed evening peak window (16:00–19:00) and out of the 18:00–21:30 period in which average demand is highest (Section 4.5), and by how much compared with Std households.  
* For example: a drop between 16:00 and 19:00 with a matching rise between 19:00 and 21:30 would only move load into the busiest hours of the day, while a matching rise after 22:00 would relieve the peak.

## **6.2 Price Event Response and Rebound (Half-Hourly Profile Chart)** {#6.2-price-event-response-and-rebound-(half-hourly-profile-chart)}

* For each half-hour of 2013, the gap between dToU and Std consumption under High and Low prices will be compared with the same gap under Normal prices. This is the main difference-in-differences estimate.  
* This measures how much dToU households cut use during High events, how much they add during Low events, and how much demand rebounds in the half-hours just before and after an event.  
* Comparing total daily consumption between dToU and Std households on days with a High event and on days with no event separates load shifting, where the cut returns as rebound, from genuine reduction, where it does not.  
* For example: a 10% cut during a High event followed by a 10% rise straight afterwards would save no energy. It would relieve the network only if the rebound falls outside the peak.

## **6.3 Response Over Time and by Temperature (Treatment Effect Chart)** {#6.3-response-over-time-and-by-temperature-(treatment-effect-chart)}

* The event effect will be plotted with confidence intervals for each month of 2013 and for each temperature band.  
* The monthly view shows whether households keep responding or lose interest as the tariff becomes routine.  
* The temperature view tests whether response weakens in cold weather, when heating cannot be delayed. If so, dynamic pricing works least well exactly when the network is under most strain.

## **6.4 Household Segments (Cluster Profiles)** {#6.4-household-segments-(cluster-profiles)}

* K-Means clustering on normalised 2013 daily load profiles from Normal-price days will group households by the shape of their ordinary consumption. Each household's High-price days are then assigned to the nearest cluster, to show whether its consumption shape changes under a price event. For households with enough 2012 readings, moves between clusters from 2012 to 2013 are also tracked.  
* This shows which consumption shapes respond to price events, and whether the overall effect comes from a few strong responders or many mild ones. Because profiles are normalised by total usage, clustering captures changes in timing, not in amount. The split between shifting and reduction comes from Section 6.2.  
* Tariff assignment is unbalanced across ACORN groups (χ² \= 23.95, df \= 2, p \= 6.3 × 10⁻⁶, excluding the 51 unclassified households; Section 4.5): 22.4% of Affluent and 21.4% of Comfortable households were on dToU, against 16.4% of Adversity households. Segments are therefore compared within each ACORN group. This shows whether response to dynamic pricing comes mainly from households that are already better able to shift their use.

## **6.5 Prediction of Responsive Households (Feature Importance Chart)** {#6.5-prediction-of-responsive-households-(feature-importance-chart)}

* A classification model will predict which dToU households respond. It uses only features not directly affected by event signals: ACORN group, consumption on Normal-price days, Normal-day load-profile cluster (Section 6.4), and weather sensitivity estimated on Normal-price days.  
* Feature importance will show which characteristics matter most. We expect how a household uses electricity on ordinary days to predict its response better than its socio-economic group. Two limitations apply. Normal-day features of dToU households may still reflect habits formed under the tariff. The response label is also measured against the same Normal-day baseline used as a feature, so part of the relationship may be mechanical (regression to the mean).  
* For example: suppliers could offer dynamic tariffs first to households with a strong evening peak rather than enrolling everyone. If the model cannot predict response, targeting is not feasible.

## 6.6 Implications for Thai Residential TOU {#6.6-implications-for-thai-residential-tou}

* MEA and PEA's residential TOU rate has a fixed weekday peak from 09:00 to 22:00 (EPPO, n.d.). No household in the London data faced a fixed-window tariff, so the results cannot estimate response to Thai TOU directly. The fixed evening-peak result (Section 6.1) is closest in form, although it rests on the 835 ToU households with at least 6 usable months of 2012 rather than all 1,123.  
* The results will show which household loads can be moved, not a direct estimate of Thai savings, since Thai demand is driven by cooling and the Thai peak lasts 13 hours.
